question: You are doing visual and mechanical checks on a new 600 V fused safety switch. Which item comes from the ATS 7.5.1.1 inspection list rather than its electrical tests?
choices: Contact resistance across each blade and fuseholder
Insulation resistance across each open pole
Blade alignment, penetration, and travel stops
Resistance of each installed fuse
explanation: ATS keeps the mechanical checks (alignment, penetration, stops, operation) in the inspection list. Blade contact resistance, insulation resistance across open poles, and fuse resistance are all electrical tests in part B. Source: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.5.1.1.A.5.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.5.1.1.A.5

question: During inspection of a fused switch, ATS 7.5.1.1 says the fuse sizes and types must agree with:
choices: The drawings and the fault and coordination studies
Whatever spare fuses are stocked in the cabinet
The largest fuse the clips will physically accept
The ampere rating printed on the switch door, and nothing else
explanation: The check is against the design: the drawings plus the short-circuit and coordination studies. A fuse that fits the clips can still be the wrong class or rating for the available fault current. Source: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.5.1.1.A.6.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.5.1.1.A.6

question: On a low-voltage air switch, the insulation-resistance test in ATS 7.5.1.1 covers each phase to the others and to ground with the blades closed. What else does it cover?
choices: Only from the line lugs to the enclosure
From each fuse clip to the neutral bar only
Across the operating handle to ground
Across each open pole
explanation: The open-pole reading proves the switch actually isolates when it is open. Test voltage and minimum value come from the manufacturer or Table 100.1, one minute. Source: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.5.1.1.B.3.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.5.1.1.B.3

question: What makes a fuse current-limiting?
choices: It contains a time-delay element that rides through motor inrush
It clears within a half-cycle, before the peak
It is built only in ratings above 600 A
It opens all three phases when any one element melts
explanation: A current-limiting fuse extinguishes the arc within the first half-cycle, so the fault current never reaches its prospective peak. A non-current-limiting fuse may melt fast but cannot clear the arc that quickly. Opening all three phases is the job of an anti-single-phase feature on fused switchgear, not of the fuse. Source: Gill, Electrical Power Equipment Maintenance and Testing, 2nd ed., 8.4.
reference: Gill, Electrical Power Equipment Maintenance and Testing, 2nd ed., 8.4

question: A 480 V main bolted-pressure switch carries 3000 A fuses in a single large cartridge size. Which UL class covers 600 V current-limiting fuses rated 601 A through 6000 A?
choices: Class H
Class L
Class CC
Class J
explanation: Gill's fuse table lists Class L at 600 V ac, 601 to 6000 A, 200 kA interrupting. Classes J and CC stop at 600 A and 30 A; Class H is a non-current-limiting fuse up to 600 A. Source: Gill, Electrical Power Equipment Maintenance and Testing, 2nd ed., 8.4.1, Table 8.1.
reference: Gill, Electrical Power Equipment Maintenance and Testing, 2nd ed., 8.4.1, Table 8.1

question: Fuses on a three-phase circuit act as single-pole interrupters. When one fuse clears and the others do not, the hazard to a running motor is:
choices: Loss of the equipment ground on that circuit
An overvoltage on the neutral that trips the GFCI
Nothing, because the other two fuses will follow within one cycle
Single phasing, with negative-sequence current heating the rotor
explanation: One open phase leaves the motor single-phased. The negative-sequence current that follows overheats the rotor and shortens motor life. Fused switchgear often adds an anti-single-phase device that opens all three poles when one fuse blows. Source: Gill, Electrical Power Equipment Maintenance and Testing, 2nd ed., 8.4.1.
reference: Gill, Electrical Power Equipment Maintenance and Testing, 2nd ed., 8.4.1

question: Which low-voltage switch is meant only for isolation and should be opened only after another device has interrupted the load?
choices: An isolating switch
A fused safety switch
An interrupter switch
A bolted-pressure switch
explanation: Gill describes three groups. An isolating switch has no interrupting or load-carrying duty. A safety switch is a quick-make, quick-break load-break switch. An interrupter switch is rated to interrupt well above its continuous current and carries a horsepower rating. Source: Gill, Electrical Power Equipment Maintenance and Testing, 2nd ed., 8.5.1.
reference: Gill, Electrical Power Equipment Maintenance and Testing, 2nd ed., 8.5.1

question: On a 4000 A bolted-pressure service switch, short-circuit interruption is normally handled by:
choices: The switch contacts, rated like a power circuit breaker
A self-powered electronic trip unit on the main
Current-limiting fuses that are part of the switch
The upstream utility transformer fuse alone
explanation: These switches carry very high continuous current under high contact pressure, but their own interrupting rating is closer to an interrupter switch than a power breaker. Integral current-limiting fuses do the fault interrupting. Source: Gill, Electrical Power Equipment Maintenance and Testing, 2nd ed., 8.5.1.
reference: Gill, Electrical Power Equipment Maintenance and Testing, 2nd ed., 8.5.1

question: A bolted-pressure switch has a ground-fault trip accessory. Where does that trip get its operating power?
choices: The fault current itself, like a self-powered breaker trip unit
A capacitor trip device charged by the load current
A small source-side control power transformer
The station battery that serves the medium-voltage gear
explanation: Unlike breaker trip units, these accessories are not self-powered. They run from a small CPT on the line side. That is why the ground-fault test required by ATS 7.5.1.1 (per Section 7.14) should prove the whole trip path, control power included. Source: Gill, Electrical Power Equipment Maintenance and Testing, 2nd ed., 8.5.1; ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.5.1.1.B.6.
reference: Gill, Electrical Power Equipment Maintenance and Testing, 2nd ed., 8.5.1; ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.5.1.1.B.6

question: A 15 kV metal-enclosed load-interrupter switch uses fuses that have expulsion elements. Which visual and mechanical check does ATS 7.5.1.2 add for those fuses?
choices: Expulsion-limiting devices are installed
SF6 pressure is within the gauge band
The oil level in the interrupter tank is correct
Each vacuum bottle passes a magnetron test
explanation: ATS 7.5.1.2 calls for expulsion-limiting devices on every holder that has an expulsion-type element. It also checks arc-interrupter operation on the switch itself. Source: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.5.1.2.A.7.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.5.1.2.A.7

question: A 15 kV metal-enclosed interrupter switch lineup has stress-cone terminations, and the manufacturer gives no field withstand value. The maximum ac test voltage in ATS Table 100.2 is:
choices: 14 kV
25 kV
27 kV
37 kV
explanation: For metal-enclosed interrupter switchgear at 15.0 kV, Table 100.2 gives 27 kV ac with stress-cone terminations and 25 kV with IEEE 386 separable terminations. The 37 shown in that row is the dc reference value. Source: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.5.1.2.B.4 and Table 100.2.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.5.1.2.B.4 and Table 100.2

question: ATS 7.5.5 covers distribution fuse cutouts. Besides alignment and penetration, which mechanical check does it list?
choices: The vacuum interrupter wear gap
The latching mechanism
The SF6 density switch
The arc chute baffles
explanation: A cutout has to latch closed reliably and drop open when the fuse link operates. ATS lists checking the latching mechanism along with alignment, penetration, and travel stops. Source: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.5.5.A.5.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.5.5.A.5

question: A fuse has no interrupting rating marked on its barrel. Under NEC 240.60(C), what rating does that imply?
choices: 10,000 A; higher ratings must be marked
No rating, so it can't be installed
explanation: Fuses carry an interrupting-rating marking when it is other than 10,000 A, along with 'current limiting' where that applies. Breakers use a different default (5,000 A, in 240.83(C)). Source: NFPA 70-2023 (NEC), 240.60(C) and 240.83(C).

question: Why won't a Class H fuse go into a Class RK1 fuseholder built to NEC 240.60(B)?
choices: Class H fuses are longer than any 600 V holder
RK1 holders accept only 250 V fuses, and Class H is 600 V
Current-limiting holders must reject non-current-limiting fuses
The holder rejects any fuse above 30 A
explanation: 240.60(B) requires current-limiting fuseholders to refuse non-current-limiting fuses, so a low-interrupting fuse can't end up where a high fault current is available. Source: NFPA 70-2023 (NEC), 240.60(B); Gill, Electrical Power Equipment Maintenance and Testing, 2nd ed., 8.4.1, Table 8.1.
reference: NFPA 70-2023 (NEC), 240.60(B); Gill, Electrical Power Equipment Maintenance and Testing, 2nd ed., 8.4.1, Table 8.1

question: A 600 V fused switch carries 2000 A fuses on a bus with very high available fault current. Which UL fuse class fits that current, and what interrupting rating does Gill's Table 8.1 list for it?
choices: Class H, up to 600 A, 10,000 A
Class J, 0 to 600 A, 200,000 A symmetrical
Class L, 601 to 6000 A, 200,000 A symmetrical
Class K, 0 to 600 A, 50,000 A symmetrical
explanation: Class L is the current-limiting class above 600 A, rated 600 V and 200 kA symmetrical. J, T, R, and K stop at 600 A, and non-current-limiting Class H is limited to 10 kA. Source: Gill, Electrical Power Equipment Maintenance and Testing, 2nd ed., 8.4.1, Table 8.1.
reference: Gill, Electrical Power Equipment Maintenance and Testing, 2nd ed., 8.4.1, Table 8.1

question: A current-limiting fuse lets through a peak of 30 kA. Treating the let-through as a triangular wave, the rms let-through is about:
choices: 10 kA
30 kA
explanation: Gill models the let-through as a triangle, whose rms is the peak divided by √3, not by √2. 30 ÷ 1.732 ≈ 17.3 kA. Using 0.707 would overstate it at 21.2 kA. Source: Gill, Electrical Power Equipment Maintenance and Testing, 2nd ed., 7.2.2 (triangular wave).
reference: Gill, Electrical Power Equipment Maintenance and Testing, 2nd ed., 7.2.2 (triangular wave)

question: On a 480 V system, Gill takes the first half-cycle rms asymmetrical current as 1.4 times the symmetrical and the peak as 1.7 times the asymmetrical. With 20 kA symmetrical available, the half-cycle peak is about:
choices: 28 kA
34 kA
40 kA
48 kA
explanation: 1.4 × 1.7 ≈ 2.4 times the symmetrical rms. 20 × 2.4 = 48 kA. A current-limiting fuse clears before the current reaches that peak. Source: Gill, Electrical Power Equipment Maintenance and Testing, 2nd ed., 7.2.2 (first half-cycle current).
reference: Gill, Electrical Power Equipment Maintenance and Testing, 2nd ed., 7.2.2 (first half-cycle current)

question: Fuse resistances on one switch read 0.50, 0.52 and 0.60 mΩ. Under ATS 7.5.1.1, what is the call?
choices: Investigate the 0.60 mΩ fuse: it is 20% above 0.50 mΩ
Acceptable: all three are under 1 mΩ
Investigate only 0.52 mΩ, the middle value
Acceptable: the limit is 50% of the lowest
explanation: ATS has you investigate fuse resistances that deviate from each other by more than 15%. 0.60 ÷ 0.50 = 1.20. The 50% rule is for contact and bolted-connection resistance, not fuses. Source: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025, 7.5.1.1.B.4 and D.4.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025, 7.5.1.1.B.4 and D.4

question: A 600 V fused switch has no manufacturer's insulation data. Which test voltage and minimum does ATS Table 100.1 give for it?
choices: 500 V dc, 25 MΩ
explanation: Table 100.1 lists 1,000 V dc and 100 MΩ for 600 V equipment. ATS 7.5.1.1 takes one-minute readings on every pole, between phases and to ground with the switch closed, plus across every open pole. Source: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025, 7.5.1.1.B.3 and D.3; Table 100.1.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025, 7.5.1.1.B.3 and D.3; Table 100.1

question: A 1600 A fused service switch is installed. Under NEC 240.67, which option meets the arc energy reduction rule?
choices: Any Class L fuse, with no check of clearing time
Fuses clearing in 0.07 s or less at the arcing current, or a listed means
A larger fuse size so the fuse never operates on arcing faults
An arc-flash label on the switch door alone
explanation: 240.67 applies to fuses rated 1200 A or more. It asks for documentation, a method that clears fast enough at the arcing current, and performance testing on site. Source: NFPA 70-2023 (NEC), 240.67(A) and (B).

question: How must the arc energy reduction system on a 1200 A fused switch be tested when first installed?
choices: Secondary injection of the relay only, with no record
Primary injection or another approved method, with a written record
Visual inspection by the installer at startup
No test; the product listing already covers performance
explanation: 240.67(C) requires a performance test on site at first installation, done per the manufacturer's instructions, with a written record kept for the AHJ. Source: NFPA 70-2023 (NEC), 240.67(C).

question: A feeder is running well above its intended load because too many motors were added, but the insulation has not broken down. A second event is a phase-to-phase fault on the same feeder. How does the Littelfuse fundamentals paper distinguish those two overcurrents?
choices: Both events are short circuits, because any current above nameplate is defined as a short circuit
An overload is current outside the normal path, and a short circuit is a modest overcurrent confined to the conductors

The first is an overload: an overcurrent that stays in the normal current paths with no insulation breakdown. The second is a short circuit: current that has left the normal path. A properly applied fuse can provide both overload and short-circuit protection, though in some uses, such as backing up a breaker or providing motor-branch short-circuit protection, the fuse may be applied for short-circuit duty only
Fuses can be applied only for short circuits and are never used for overload protection
explanation: An overload is overcurrent that stays in the normal current paths and does not involve an insulation breakdown. Typical causes include too much connected equipment, overloaded machinery, or a mechanical breakdown such as a failed bearing. If it is not interrupted in time, a sustained overload overheats components and damages insulation. A short circuit is current that flows outside its normal path and must be interrupted quickly because of heating, magnetic stress, and arcing. When they are properly rated, fuses provide both overload and short-circuit protection. In some applications, such as backing up a breaker or providing motor-branch short-circuit and ground-fault protection, the fuses supply short-circuit protection only. Source: Littelfuse, Fuse Fundamentals, 2025, Overcurrent Types: Overloads Versus Short Circuits, and the following page on fuse opening.
reference: Littelfuse, Fuse Fundamentals, 2025, Overcurrent Types: Overloads Versus Short Circuits, and the following page on fuse opening

question: A current-limiting fuse is being applied to cut let-through energy on a high available-fault bus. How quickly does the Littelfuse paper say a current-limiting fuse opens and clears a short circuit, and what energy measure is being reduced?
choices: It opens and clears in less than 180 electrical degrees, that is, in the first half cycle, and it greatly reduces the destructive heat energy expressed as I-squared-t
It is allowed three to five cycles to clear, which is still called current-limiting in the paper
Current-limiting means only that the fuse rating is less than the load current, not that clearing time or I-squared-t is reduced
A current-limiting fuse waits for the first current zero after two full cycles, then reduces voltage, not current
explanation: Current-limiting fuses cut the I-squared-t energy that reaches the circuit. They clear a short circuit in under 180 electrical degrees, meaning within the first half-cycle. Supplemental and Class K fuses are the usual exceptions; most other everyday classes used in modern systems are treated as current-limiting under that description. Peak let-through curves show how far a given fuse limits current. Because I-squared-t scales with the square of current, a tenfold current rise is a hundredfold energy rise, which is why reducing let-through current pays such a large energy dividend. Source: Littelfuse, Fuse Fundamentals, 2025, Current Limitation, and the earlier I-squared-t discussion.
reference: Littelfuse, Fuse Fundamentals, 2025, Current Limitation, and the earlier I-squared-t discussion

question: A 480 V ac bus also has a 250 V dc control circuit, and a crew wants to use the same ac-rated fuses in the dc circuit because the ac voltage rating is higher. What does the Littelfuse paper require?
choices: Any ac voltage rating higher than the dc circuit voltage is automatically acceptable on dc
Voltage rating may be ignored if the interrupting rating is 200 kA
Dc circuits may use ac-only fuses if the current rating is derated by half

A fuse's voltage rating has to be at least the highest voltage on the circuit where it is installed, and a fuse in a dc circuit must be specifically rated for dc. Using an ac-only fuse on dc, or exceeding the voltage rating, can lead to serious fuse failure
explanation: Voltage rating is the highest ac or dc voltage at which the fuse is designed to carry load and to clear overcurrent. Apply a fuse whose voltage rating is at least the highest voltage on that circuit. A fuse may be listed ac only, dc only, or both; a dc circuit needs a fuse specifically listed for dc. A lower-rated fuse, or an ac-only fuse placed on dc, can fail violently. Source: Littelfuse, Fuse Fundamentals, 2025, Voltage Rating.
reference: Littelfuse, Fuse Fundamentals, 2025, Voltage Rating

question: A new main switchboard has 125 kA available at the line terminals. The next standard fuse interrupting ratings above that value are 200 kA, and some UL listed fuses go higher still. What interrupting-rating rule does the paper apply, including the NEC 110.9 point it quotes?
choices: A fuse whose interrupting rating is 100 kA may be used on a 125 kA bus if it is current-limiting

The fuse interrupting rating at the nominal circuit voltage must be at least as high as the available short-circuit current at the equipment line terminals. A 200 kA fuse meets that 125 kA duty and leaves margin if the available current rises later. Standard UL fuses are available with interrupting ratings up to 300 kA
Interrupting rating needs only to exceed the fuse's current rating, not the available fault current
NEC 110.9 applies only to circuit breakers, so fuse interrupting rating is optional
explanation: Interrupting rating is the largest short-circuit current a fuse is listed to clear, at its rated voltage, in the laboratory tests that define the listing. A UL-listed fuse must clear every overcurrent between its ampere rating and that interrupting rating. Standard UL listings go as high as 300 kA. NEC 110.9 requires any device meant to open fault current to be listed for at least the available short-circuit current at its line-side terminals. A 200 kA interrupting rating is a common way to keep that rating adequate and to leave reserve if available current later increases. In the paper's example, a board with 125 kA available is fitted with 200 kA fuses. Source: Littelfuse, Fuse Fundamentals, 2025, Interrupting Rating, including the NEC 110.9 quotation and Figure 1.
reference: Littelfuse, Fuse Fundamentals, 2025, Interrupting Rating, including the NEC 110.9 quotation and Figure 1

question: A motor branch will use a time-delay Class R fuse. What current and time test does the Littelfuse paper say a time-delay Class R fuse must meet, and how do Class RK1 and RK5 differ in current limitation?
choices: Time-delay Class R fuses must open at 200% of rating in less than 1 second, and RK1 and RK5 have the same let-through

Time-delay fuses in this class must hold 500% of their current rating for a minimum of 10 seconds. Class R covers 0 to 600 A with a 200 kA interrupting rating. RK1 provides a high degree of current limitation; RK5 provides a moderate degree that is adequate for most applications
Class R is only a 10 kA one-time fuse and has no time-delay option
RK5 is more current-limiting than RK1 and is preferred whenever Type 2 no-damage protection of a starter is required
explanation: UL Class R is covered by UL 248-12, with voltage ratings of 250 V and 600 V ac (and listed dc ratings), current ratings from 0 to 600 A, and a 200 kA rms symmetrical interrupting rating. The class splits into RK1 and RK5. Time delay is optional for Class R; when a fuse is a time-delay type it must hold 500% of its current rating for a minimum of 10 seconds. RK1 offers a high degree of current limitation and can provide IEC Type 2 (no-damage) protection for motor starters and controls. RK5 offers a moderate degree of current limitation that is adequate for most applications. Class R fuses fit rejection holders that will not accept a non-Class R fuse. Source: Littelfuse, Fuse Fundamentals, 2025, UL and CSA Fuse Classes, Class R.
reference: Littelfuse, Fuse Fundamentals, 2025, UL and CSA Fuse Classes, Class R

question: A selectively coordinated fused service uses Littelfuse POWR-PRO and POWR-GARD fuses. A 400 A time-delay RK1 feeder will supply a 50 A time-delay RK5 branch. Using only the paper's coordination table for those series, is that pair coordinated, and what I-squared-t rule is the table built on?
choices: Any 2:1 ratio is enough for every fuse pair, including RK1 over RK5, regardless of class or manufacturer
RK1 and RK5 cannot be coordinated with each other at any ratio
Selective coordination is determined only by current rating, and I-squared-t is not used

The table lists an 8:1 line-to-load ratio for a time-delay RK1 supplying a time-delay RK5, so 400 A to 50 A (8:1) meets that row. The underlying rule is that the smaller fuse's total-clearing I-squared-t must be less than the larger fuse's melting I-squared-t. This table is for the listed Littelfuse series, not a universal ratio for every manufacturer's fuses
explanation: For a system to be coordinated, the smaller fuse's total-clearing I-squared-t must be less than the larger fuse's melting I-squared-t, so the downstream fuse opens before the upstream element is damaged. Melting and total-clearing curves can be compared, but the simplest method in the paper is its fuse coordination table, which applies only to the listed Littelfuse POWR-PRO and POWR-GARD series. That table gives an 8:1 line-to-load ratio for time-delay RK1 (LLNRK / LLSRK_ID) over time-delay RK5 (FLNR_ID / FLSR_ID / IDSR). A 400 A RK1 over a 50 A RK5 is exactly 8:1. By contrast, Class L to Class L, and Class L to RK1 or Class J, are shown at 2:1 for those same series. Do not treat those ratios as a generic rule for every brand. Source: Littelfuse, Fuse Fundamentals, 2025, Fuse Selectivity and Table 2.
reference: Littelfuse, Fuse Fundamentals, 2025, Fuse Selectivity and Table 2
